Deep learning-based methods utilizing 3D LiDAR data have significantly advanced the field of 3D orientation and positioning. This paper introduces Attention-driven LiDOR Downsampling (LiDOR-DL) and Attentive-driven LiDOR-Network (AdLiDOR-N), enhancing rendering-based feature extraction for 3D orientation and location recognition. In these frameworks, points within a map are first clustered via LiDOR, which samples points attentively. This process generates a compact cloud containing more semantic information than standard LiDOR, enabling rapid processing. Subsequently, these enhanced clusters are encoded into global features using PointNet++ and global max-pooling. Finally, a full connection layer combined with a spatial temporal Bi-LM extracts local and integrated context from current and previous maps to predict the 3D orientation and location. Key advantages of these architectures include a reduced number of parameters, higher processing speed, and superior performance. We evaluated these algorithms across four public datasets, demonstrating their efficacy.

Imitation learning (IL) enables machines to acquire complex behaviors by observing human demonstrations, yet a major obstacle is designing ideal loss functions that effectively measure the gap between an agent’s output and a demonstrated action. To address this, we introduce **TR**ail: an approach that improves IL by combining a statistical model of the training data with a generative process for generating "ideal" demonstrations independent of empirical distributional limitations. We evaluate TRail on five real-world IL benchmarks, showing that it surpasses baseline methods in scenarios where IL training data is small or skewed.

Speech-emotion recognition systems leverage deep reinforcement learning to extract prosodic features from audio, mapping these characteristics to emotional labels. Although such methods demonstrate high accuracy in laboratory settings, they encounter two major hurdles when deployed with live audio streams: significant domain shifts between lab-recorded and real-world data, and the inherent scarcity of emotional training datasets. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a domain-adaptive deep reinforcement learning framework tailored for speech-emotion classification. The domain adaptation component employs a feature alignment strategy to minimize statistical discrepancies in attributes like pitch between source and target domains. Meanwhile, the small-sample learning component functions as a density-level method that utilizes vast unlabeled real-world speech data for adaptation while requiring only five labeled examples as seeds. Experimental results utilizing real-world datasets validate that this proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art accuracy benchmarks.

This study employs high-pressure nuclear forward scattering to investigate the unique transition in the magnetic properties of Aurivillius phase $\text{Bi}_5\text{FeTi}_3\text{O}_{15}$ (a structure where a perovskite layer is substituted with a single perovskite layer of a different cation). By subjecting a three-layered Fe-doped Bi$_{5}$FTO to pressures up to roughly $13.5~\text{GPa}$ and analyzing the magnetic scalar scattering, we identified a central transition where antiferromagnetism converts to ferromagnetism. Notably, the pressure-induced ferromagnetic state persists even after the system returns to ambient conditions, implying a switch to self-constructed magnetic ordering. These findings offer fresh insights regarding pressure-assisted phase transities in multi-layered systems and their potential impact on the development of new spin-based applications using the Aurivillius phase.

This work addresses a distributed optimization challenge among a group of communication partners in digital networks, where a specific subset acts as malicious nodes and attempts to drive the optimization process toward suboptimal outcomes. These adversaries possess limited access to the communication channels and lack direct knowledge of the objective function. The proposed developed algorithm implements an encrypted communication framework grounded in a distributed quantized technique tailored for gradient descent, specifically robust against these hostile actions. Analysis demonstrates that under certain conditions, the healthy nodes will either reach a precise stationary point or get sufficiently close to a stationary point of the specific convex objective function, provided that a combination of distributed communication noise and quantization noise remains favorable. Finally, performance metrics are validated through numerical simulations based on actual power system load scenarios.

Developing robust simulations of instrumental and systematic effects in the observation of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) is vital for analyzing data from present and future experiments. The s4cmb library, built on Python, s4, and YAMLEmpy, facilitates this by generating realistic end-to-end simulations that incorporate modern experiments' intricate features. This capability supports both the creation of synthetic datasets for experimental planning and analysis code development, as well as processing real observations. To demonstrate its capabilities, this paper employs s4cmb to generate simulated time-ordered data emulating Planck's 2018 legacy data using full Planck instrumental models, achieving a successful replication of the residual foreground residuals and the Cosmic Microwave Background power spectrum characteristic of the original Planck analysis.

Large, language-model-driven networks have become prominent in natural language processing, offering significant advantages. This study examines their utility specifically in word ordering tasks. While prior research generally held that these models provide only minimal generalizability beyond their training data, we challenge this view through a detailed analysis of the BART model. Investigating various word permutation tasks, we observe that task success heavily relies on specific training data and post-processing methods rather than broad linguistic capabilities. Furthermore, our findings offer a proposed framework aimed at future research into the capabilities and training strategies of language models.

Deepfake technology utilizes advanced algorithms to synthesize realistic content, posing significant threats to society. Although numerous models exist, they frequently fail to generalize across diverse testing environments, often due to an over-reliance on specific feature representations. To mitigate these issues and enhance robustness, we introduce a Multi-Domain Cross-Strengthened Network (MD-CSDNetwork). This proposed framework integrates three key mechanisms: Feature Enrichment, which supplies complementary information from various models to boost deepening capabilities; Adaptive Instance Normalization, which improves deep features; and the core Multi-Domain Cross-Sewn Network architecture, which enriches representation by aggregating activations from different representations. Conducted experiments using the DFDC and FaceForensics++ datasets confirm that MD-CSDNetwork achieves state-ofthe-art performance, proving its superior deepening performance and robustness.

Low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes employ a two-dimensional degree-degree linked layout, where the bit-node and check-node degree distributions are governed independently yet remain associated through a specific functional relationship. Our methodology leverages an entropy minimization tree to characterize the threshold for successful decoding, revealing that the link between bit-node and check-node degree distributions markedly influences decoding performance across various erasure channels.

Establishing a robust and user-friendly environment for representing and analyzing multidimensional vector data is fundamental to numerous sectors, including finance, insurance, and marketing. Yet, as data dimensionality expands, conventional visualization methods often prove inadequate or cannot be applied at all. While specialized tools like ViDaExpert offer capabilities for low-dimensional visualization of large datasets across numerous attributes, they have historically relied on manually crafted, industry-specific tables. This manual dependency restricts flexibility and increases development time. To address this, we introduce a low-cost, automated, and streamlined procedure for automatically designing representation interfaces. This method leverages an autonomous, evolutionary algorithm to generate expert-level tables that reflect the structure of high-dimensional data. Consequently, manual intervention is largely eliminated, allowing for significant reduction in representation and development efforts. Multiple real-world cases demonstrate the system's effectiveness, highlighting how such methodologies support expert decision-making in various fields.
